div.p: A federated approach to the multiprocessor scheduling of systems of independent recurrent tasks is considered, in which each task is either restricted to execute preemptively upon a single processor, or may execute upon multiple processors but gets exclusive access to all these processors. Efficient polynomial-time algorithms are derived here for the federated schedulability analysis and run-time scheduling of recurrent task systems that are represented by the conditional sporadic DAG tasks model. The performance of these algorithms is characterized via a speedup factor metric, which quantifies the combined cost of both restricting oneself to the federated scheduling paradigm, and of requiring the scheduling algorithms to run in polynomial time.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: This paper discusses the federated scheduling of recurrent real-time systems that are modeled as collections of independent conditional sporadic DAG tasks. We now describe this scope in greater detail below.

Conditional Sporadic DAG tasks. The origins of the discipline of real-time scheduling theory is often traced to the widely-cited paper [20] by Liu and Layland, concerning the schedulability analysis of systems modeled using what is now referred to as the Liu & Layland task model. Since that seminal piece of work, a series of successive generalizations to the basic task model have been proposed, including the 3-parameter sporadic task model [23], the multiframe task model [24], the generalized multiframe task model [10], and the non-cyclic generalized multiframe task model [25]. All these models are able to represent, to varying degrees of accuracy, recurrent processes that can be thought of as abstractions of straight-line code embedded within an in-finite loop and therefore capable of generating potentially unbounded sequences of pieces of work (referred to as jobs).

However, code found in actual real-time systems is not always straight-line; it may include conditional statements (such as if-then-else constructs). Steps towards modeling such conditional real-time code began in the mid-1990's, when the recurring branching tasks model [1] was proposed; this was soon generalized to models including the recurring real-time tasks model [2], etc., culminating eventually in the digraph task model [28]; see [27] for an excellent survey on the topic of models for representing recurrent real-time processes.

All the models mentioned above were developed in the context of uniprocessor systems. However, it is increasingly the case that most real-time systems, including highly safety-critical ones, are coming to be implemented upon multicore and multiprocessor platforms. And with this move to multiprocessor implementations, the real-time systems community is increasingly coming to recognize that the kinds of workloads found in modern real-time systems often possess considerable parallelism, which should be exploited in order to enhance feasibility -i.e., make it more likely that we will be able to construct scheduling strategies that meet all deadlines. But the models described above make no effort to expose intra-task parallelism-the work generated by each individual recurrent task is assumed to be completely sequential, and any particular task is allowed to execute upon at most one processor at each instant in time. This shortcoming of prior models has given rise to a need for new models for representing recurrent real-time processes that are capable or modeling intra-task parallelism, thereby exposing such parallelism for potential exploitation by run-time scheduling mechanisms. Some models of this kind that have been proposed include the moldable tasks model [21], the malleable tasks model [14], and the fork-join or parallel synchronous task model [16]; the sporadic DAG tasks model [9] (see [7,Chapter 21] for a text-book description) is a generalization of these models. A task τi in the sporadic DAG tasks model is specified as a 3-tuple (Gi, Di, Ti), where Gi is a directed acyclic graph (DAG), and Di and Ti are positive integers representing the relative deadline and period parameters of τi respectively. The task τi repeatedly releases dag-jobs, each of which is a collection of (sequential) jobs. Successive dag-jobs are released a duration of at least Ti time units apart. The DAG Gi is specified as Gi = (Vi, Ei), where Vi is a set of vertices and Ei a set of directed edges between these vertices. Each v ∈ Vi represents the execution of a sequential piece of code (a "job"), and is characterized by a worst-case execution time (wcet). The edges represent dependencies between the jobs: if (v1, v2) ∈ Ei then job v1 must complete execution before job v2 can begin execution. (Job v1 is called a predecessor job of v2, and job v2 is called a successor job of v1.) Jobs that are not predecessors or successors of each other, either directly or transitively, may execute simultaneously upon different processors. A release of a dag-job of τi at time-instant t means that all |Vi| jobs v ∈ Vi are released at time-instant t. If a dag-job is released at time-instant t then all |Vi| jobs that were released at t must complete execution by time-instant t + Di.

As stated above, the sporadic DAG tasks model assumes that each release of a dag-job of τi causes the release of jobs corresponding to each and every vertex in Vi. It is thus successful in modeling intra-task parallelism: the workload generated by an individual task may comprise multiple jobs that are allowed to execute in parallel upon different processors. However, control structures (such as conditional -if-then-else -constructs) within the code that is being modeled by the task may mean that different activations of the task (i.e., different dag-jobs) cause different parts of the code to be executed. Assuming that jobs corresponding to all the vertices in Vi will execute during each such activation is pessimistic; there is a need to be able to model the fact that different dag-jobs of the same task may cause different collections of jobs to be executed. The conditional sporadic DAG tasks model [8,22] therefore further generalized the sporadic DAG tasks model by allowing for the representation of conditional execution of parts of a DAG; we will describe this model in detail in Section 2. Federated scheduling. Real-time systems have traditionally been implemented upon multiprocessor platforms using either a partitioned or a global scheduling algorithm. In the partitioned approach, each task gets mapped on to a processor prior to run-time; during run-time, all jobs generated by a task may execute only upon the processor to which the task has been mapped. In the global approach, by contrast, different jobs of the same task may execute upon different processors, and if preemption is permitted then a preempted job may resume execution upon a processor different from the one on which it had previously been executing. It has been observed that as a general rule, partitioned scheduling has the advantage of simplicity of analysis and implementation, whereas global scheduling allows for the use of a larger fraction of the total platform computing capacity.

The notions of partitioned and global scheduling pre-date the introduction of task models capable of representing multithreaded tasks. It is clear that the global approach is also applicable to task systems represented using the task models that permit intra-task parallelism; a number of papers (e.g., [26,18,9,13,3]) have studied the global scheduling of such task systems. However, it is not immediately evident what the natural analog of partitioned scheduling should be for systems represented using these models. If we were to restrict all jobs of a task to execute upon only a single processor, we would not be able to take advantage of the parallelism within individual tasks that is the raison d'être for the sporadic DAG and related models; additionally, such a restriction would hobble the expressiveness of the model considerably by forbidding the existence of "heavy" tasks -i.e., tasks with a (parallelizable) computational demand exceeding the capacity of a single processor to accommodate it. An interesting idea, termed federated scheduling, was introduced in [19]; under federated scheduling, it is required that each heavy task be granted exclusive access to all the processors upon which it executes. All the processors can therefore be considered to be partitioned into clusters numbering one plus the number of heavy tasks, with each heavy task executing upon a dedicated cluster and all the remaining (non-heavy) tasks executing upon a shared cluster. Later works on federated scheduling (e.g. [5,6]) added a further dimension to the notion of federated scheduling: under the resulting extended definition, tasks that are permitted to execute upon more than one processor are granted exclusive access to the processors upon which they execute, while the remaining tasks are partitioned amongst a pool of shared processors. (Hence each task executing upon a shared processor executes on one processor only.) Since in this paper we are looking upon federated scheduling as a generalization of partitioned scheduling, it makes sense to restrict the scheduling of the tasks that may share processors to in this manner, and we will do so. The simplicity of partitioned scheduling is thus maintained, while we will see that for some task models the capacity loss due to partitioning is capped at no larger a fraction of the platform capacity than was the case with partitioned scheduling of sequential tasks.

This research. In this paper, we seek to study the applicability of the federated scheduling paradigm to the scheduling of conditional sporadic DAG task systems. Doing so by extending prior results that were originally derived for the federated scheduling of non-conditional sporadic DAG task systems turns out to be quite challenging. This is due in large part to the fact that a single conditional sporadic DAG task may have exponentially many different execution paths through it; consider for example code that is structured in the following manner: where each (Ci) represents a boolean condition, and each {Sij} a block of straight-line code. It is evident that such a code fragment may have 2 n different execution flows through it; explicitly considering each such path separately would lead to computationally infeasible (exponential-time) algorithms. We derive a polynomial-time algorithm for determining the number of processors that should be devoted to an individual conditional sporadic DAG task so as to be able to guarantee that it always meets its deadline upon these processors, regardless of which execution path it takes through its code during run-time; we prove the efficacy of our algorithm via the speedup factor metric. Tasks with cumulative computational requirement modest enough to be accommodated upon a single processor do not need to be executed upon multiple processors; such tasks are transformed to tasks in the traditional 3-parameter sporadic task model [23], and partitioned using previously-proposed algorithms for partitioning systems of such tasks.

div.head: CONDITIONAL SPORADIC DAG TASKS
div.p: We now describe the conditional sporadic DAG task model, which was proposed in [8,22] as a generalization to the traditional sporadic DAG tasks as described in Section 1 above. As with traditional sporadic tasks, each conditional sporadic DAG task τi is specified as a 3-tuple (Gi, Di, Ti), where Gi = (Vi, Ei) is a DAG, and Di and Ti are positive integers. We require that Gi have a single source vertex and a single sink vertex. 1 Conditional vertices are special vertices in Vi that are defined in pairs. Let (c1, c2) be such a pair in the DAG Gi = (Vi, Ei) -see Figure 1. Informally speaking, vertex c1 can be thought of representing a point in the code where a conditional expression is evaluated and, depending upon the outcome of this evaluation, control will subsequently flow along exactly one of several different possible paths in the code. It is required that all these different paths meet again at a common point in the code, represented by the vertex c2. More formally, 1. There are multiple outgoing edges from c1 in Ei. Suppose that there are exactly k outgoing edges from c1 to the vertices s1, s2, . . . , s k , for some k > 1. We call k the branching factor of this conditional. Then there are exactly k incoming edges into c2 in Ei, from the vertices t1, t2, . . . , t k , 2. For each ∈ {1, 2, . . . , k}, let V ⊆ Vi and E ⊆ Ei denote all the vertices and edges on paths reachable from s that do not include vertex c2. By definition, s is the sole source vertex of the DAG G def = (V , E ). It must hold that t is the sole sink vertex of G .

div.p: V j = ∅ for all , j, = j. Additionally, with the exception of (c1, s ) there should be no edges in Ei into vertices in V from vertices not in V , for each ∈ {1, 2, . . . , k}. I.e., Ei ((Vi \ V ) × V ) = {(c1, s )} should hold for all .

Edges (v1, v2) between pairs of vertices neither of which are conditional vertices represent precedence constraints exactly as in traditional sporadic DAG tasks, while edges involving conditional vertices represent conditional execution of code. More specifically, let (c1, c2) denote a defined pair of conditional vertices (recall that conditional vertices are always defined in pairs). The semantics of conditional DAG task execution mandate that • After the job c1 completes execution, exactly one of its successor jobs becomes eligible to execute; it is not known beforehand which successor job may execute.
• Job c2 begins to execute upon the completion of exactly one of its predecessor jobs.

The branching factor for an "if-then-else" condition is 2. Without loss of generality, we will assume in this paper that all conditionals have branching factor 2; conditionals with branching factor > 2 can always be converted to an equivalent sequence of conditionals with branching factor two with no more than a polynomial increase in the size of the DAG.

Some additional terminology: for each pair (c1, c2) of conditional vertices in Gi, we refer to the subgraph of Gi beginning at c1 and ending at c2 as a conditional construct in Gi. Each conditional construct represents a branching choice in the code that is being modeled by Gi. A canonical conditional construct with branching factor 2 is depicted pictorially in Figure 1. It is permitted in our model that conditional constructs be nested: a conditional construct may contain additional conditional constructs within it. We use the term inner-most conditional construct to denote a conditional construct that does not contain any conditional constructs within it. The DAG for an example conditional sporadic DAG task is depicted in Figure 2. Small solid circles denote "dummy" vertices, which correspond to jobs with wcet equal to zero. Diamond and oval vertices denote start and end conditional vertices, respectively; there are two pairs of conditional vertices in this DAG, each with branching factor equal to two. (For those reading this on a color medium, the upper conditional construct is represented in blue; the lower conditional construct in red.) The semantics of this DAG task are as follows. Whenever a dag-job is released, the dummy source vertex has zero execution requirement and therefore immediately completes execution. Two vertices, with wcets 3 and 6 respectively, both become eligible for execution. Once both these jobs have completed, three jobs become eligible simultaneously.

• A conditional expression with a wcet of 1 is evaluated; depending upon the outcome of this evaluation, either three jobs each with wcet equal to 8, or two jobs each with wcet equal to 10, are executed.
After these jobs complete, a single job with wcet equal to 12 is executed.

• Another conditional expression that has a wcet of 2 is evaluated. Depending upon the outcome of this evaluation, either a single job with a wcet equal to 8, or two jobs with wcet equal to 4 and 6 respectively, are executed.
• A single job with wcet equal to 12 is executed.

We seek to schedule a given collection of n conditional sporadic DAG tasks τ1, τ2, . . . , τn upon m unit-speed processors. In this paper, we restrict our attention to constrained deadline systems: those in which Di ≤ Ti for all tasks τi in the system. Our interest is in the federated scheduling of this task system; i.e., we seek to 1. First, determine which of the tasks are to be assigned multiple processors for their exclusive use, and which are to execute on single processors (that will perhaps be shared with other tasks).
2. For those that are to execute exclusively on multiple processors, determine how many processors to assign to each such task.
3. For the remaining tasks -those that are to be partitioned amongst the remaining processors -determine such a partitioning of the tasks.
Some additional notation and terminology:
Figure 1: A canonical conditional construct with branching factor 2. Vertices s1 and t1 (vertices s2 and t2, resp.) are the sole source vertex and sink vertex of G 1 (G 2 , resp.).

• A chain in conditional sporadic DAG task τi is a sequence of vertices v1, v2, . . . , v k ∈ Vi such that (vj, vj+1) is an edge in Gi, 1 ≤ j < k. The length of this chain is defined to be the sum of the wcets of all the vertices in the chain. We denote by leni the length of the longest chain in the DAG Gi. Observe that leni denotes the maximum duration of time any dag-job of τi may take to complete execution, if it were to execute upon an unbounded number of unit-speed processors. For our example conditional sporadic DAG task τ1 of Figure 2, len1 = (6 + 1 + 10 + 0 + 12) = 29.

• Let Ji denote all possible complete collections of jobs that comprise a single dag-job of τi, along with the precedence constraints amongst these jobs that are imposed by the edges Ei. Thus each J ∈ Ji denotes a collection of precedence-constrained jobs obtained by completely executing through the DAG Gi once, taking into account the conditional branches within it. As stated in Section 1, there may in general be exponentially many different flows through a graph; hence the number of precedence-constrained collections of jobs in Ji (denoted |Ji|) may be exponential in the number of vertices in Gi.

• Let voli be the maximum total wcet of a dag-job that could be generated by τi, taking into account the conditional branches within it. I.e., voli is the maximum, over all J ∈ Ji, of the sum of the wcets of all the jobs in J; equivalently, voli denotes the maximum amount of execution that could be required by any one dag-job of τi.

For our example DAG task τ1 of Figure 2, a dag-job has maximum total wcet if the upper branch (1 + (8 × 3) + 0 = 25) is taken for the upper conditional, and the lower branch (2 + (4 + 6) + 0 = 12) for the lower conditional. The total maximum wcet is therefore 6 + 3 + 25 + 12 + 12 + 12 = 70, meaning that vol1 = 70.

We will see in Section 3 that the efficient computation of leni and voli are essential components of our federated schedulability analysis algorithm for systems of conditional sporadic DAG tasks. We now discuss how these quantities may be computed efficiently.

Computing leni. Given a conditional sporadic DAG task τi, the quantity leni is easily computed in time linear in the representation of the task, as follows. Observe that leni is the largest cumulative wcet of all the vertices in any chain in the DAG Gi from the source vertex to the sink vertex in Gi (both vertices included). This can be determined by first obtaining a topological sorting of the vertices in Gi, and then considering the vertices in topological order. In considering a vertex, we seek to compute the largest cumulative wcet of all the vertices in any chain from the source vertex to the vertex under consideration.
• When the source vertex in being considered, this value is simply equal to its wcet.
• For every vertex subsequently considered, this value is equal to the wcet of the vertex plus the maximum of the values computed for all its (immediate) predecessor vertices.

The last vertex considered is the sink vertex, and the value computed as the largest cumulative wcet of all the vertices in any chain from the source vertex to this sink vertex gives us the desired quantity leni.

Computing voli. By definition, voli is the maximum, over all J ∈ Ji, of the total wet of all the jobs in J. But since |Ji| may be exponential for a conditional DAG task, directly applying the definition will yield an exponential-time algorithm for computing volume. For a traditional (nonconditional) sporadic DAG task τi, |Ji| = 1 and the volume of τi is simply equal to the sum of the wcet parameters of all the vertices in the DAG Gi of τi. Below we describe a polynomial-time algorithm for transforming a conditional sporadic DAG task τi to a non-conditional sporadic DAG task τ i with the same volume; by first applying this algorithm to τi and then computing the volume of τ i , voli may be determined in polynomial time for the conditional sporadic DAG task τi.

Let τi = (Gi, Di, Ti) denote a conditional sporadic DAG task, and τ i = (G i , D i , T i ) the non-conditional sporadic DAG task with the same volume that we seek to obtain. D i ← Di, and T i ← Ti. To obtain G i , we start out with the DAG Gi and repeatedly 1. identify an innermost conditional construct; and 2. replace this conditional construct with a single (normal, not conditional) vertex that has wcet equal to the sum of the wcets of the two conditional vertices plus the larger of the sum of the wcet's of the two branches. (The large rectangle encloses a single conditional construct in the DAG that will be referenced later in this document.)
until there are no remaining conditional constructs in the DAG. We illustrate on the example of Figure 2.

• Suppose that during the first iteration we identify the upper conditional construct -the one demarcated by a large rectangle. Traversing this conditional construct via the upper branch would result in a wcet of (1+8×3) or 25, while traversing it through the lower branch would result in a wcet of (1 + 2 × 10) or 21. We therefore replace the upper conditional construct by a single vertex with wcet equal to max (25,21) or 25.

• During the second iteration we will identify the lower conditional construct. Traversing this conditional construct via the upper branch would result in a wcet of (2 + 8) or 10, while traversing it through the lower branch would result in a wcet of (2 + (6 + 4)) or 12.
We therefore replace the lower conditional construct by a single vertex with wcet equal to max(10, 12) or 12.
• There are no remaining conditional constructs. The volume of the resulting (non-conditional) DAG is equal to the sum of the wcets of all the nodes in the DAG, or 3 + 6 + 25 + 12 + 12 + 12, or 70.

div.head: A SCHEDULING ALGORITHM
div.p: We now describe and discuss Algorithm FedSched, our algorithm for the federated scheduling of a constrained deadline conditional sporadic DAG task system τ upon a multiprocessor platform of m unit-speed processors. As stated in Section 2 above, Algorithm FedSched 1. First determines which of the tasks are to be assigned multiple processors for their exclusive use, and which are to execute on single processors.
2. For those that are to execute exclusively on multiple processors, it determines how many processors to assign to each such task.
3. For the remaining tasks -those that are to be partitioned amongst the remaining processors -it determines an appropriate partitioning of the tasks.

In order to achieve these goals, Algorithm FedSched starts out by computing the leni and voli parameters for each task τi in the task system τ . The voli values are used as the basis for classifying all the tasks in τ as being either light or heavy. Any τi satisfying the constraint that voli ≤ Di is classified as a light task; the remaining tasks are heavy tasks.
Let τ light ⊆ τ denote all the light tasks in τ , and τ heavy def = (τ \ τ light ) denote the heavy tasks in τ . Algorithm Fed-Sched (pseudo-code in Figure 3) first determines how many

if (mi > mr) return failure 5 mr ← mr -mi £ update the remaining number of processors end for 6 partition(τ light , mr) £ See Figure 4 end During run-time, jobs of the heavy tasks are executed upon the processors that are devoted to them as discussed below, while each shared processor is scheduled using preemptive uniprocessor Earliest Deadline First (edf).

div.head: Heavy tasks
div.p: Recall that in this paper, we are restricting our attention to systems of constrained-deadline conditional sporadic DAG tasks. Since the relative deadline of a constraineddeadline task is no larger than its period, all the jobs of one dag-job of the task must complete execution before the next dag-job is released. To ensure that τi will always meet all its deadlines upon a number of processors that are dedicated to its exclusive use, we must ensure that each J ∈ Ji completes execution upon these processors within a duration that is no greater than the relative deadline Di. For each individual J ∈ Ji, this is equivalent to scheduling J to have a makespan no larger than Di when scheduled upon the provided processors. Unfortunately, determining whether such a J can be scheduled to have makespan ≤ Di upon a given number of processors is easily shown, from results in [17], to be NP-hard in the strong sense and to remain so even when the scheduler is given a speedup < 4/3. (In fact, assuming a reasonable complexity-theoretic conjecture that is somewhat stronger than P = NP, a recent result of Svensson [29] implies that a speedup < 2 polynomial time test is ruled out.) It is however known that Graham's list scheduling algorithm (LS) [15], which essentially constructs a work-conserving schedule by always executing an available job, if any are present, upon any available processor, makes the following speedup guarantee: if there exists a schedule for J of makespan ≤ Di upon mi unit-speed processors, then LS will schedule J to have a makespan no greater than Di upon mi processors each of speed (2 -1/mi). This result, in conjunction with the hardness results of [17,29], suggests that LS is a reasonable algorithm to use for scheduling each heavy task, and we do indeed do so.

We therefore have a suitable run-time scheduling algo-rithm; however, constructing a corresponding schedulability test for these heavy tasks is not straightforward. To ensure that the heavy conditional sporadic DAG task τi will always meet all deadlines upon a given number mi of dedicated processors when LS is the run-time scheduling algorithm that is used, we must ensure that LS would schedule all J ∈ Ji upon mi processors to have a makespan no greater than Di.

Since |Ji| may in general be exponential in the representation of τ , the straightforward approach of simulating LS on all J ∈ Ji yields an exponential-time schedulability test; Lemma 1 below will be used to derive a polynomial-time one.
Lemma 1. Suppose that heavy conditional sporadic DAG task τi is assigned mi processors. Let L(J) denote the makespan when any J ∈ Ji is scheduled using LS. It holds that
div.formula: max J∈J i L(J) ≤ voli mi + 1 - 1 mi leni(1)
div.p: Proof: For each J ∈ Ji, let vol(J) denote the sum of the wcets of all the jobs in J, and len(J) the length of the longest chain in J. (Note that it follows by definition that len(J) ≤ leni, and that vol(J) ≤ voli.) Observe that under LS, some job in the longest chain must be executing at each instant that any processor is idle. Hence an upper bound on the makespan L(J) is obtained by considering that all remaining processors are idle at all instants that a job in the longest chain is executing. This occurs if an amount of work vol(J) -len(J) executes with maximum parallelism (i.e., on all mi processors), and the jobs in the longest chain execute on a single processor. The resulting makespan bound is
div.formula: vol(J) -len(J) mi + len(J) = vol(J) mi + 1 - 1 mi len(J) ≤ voli mi + 1 - 1 mi leni
div.p: and the lemma is proved.

div.head: Light tasks
div.p: In the partitioning step, multiple light conditional sporadic DAG tasks may be assigned to the same processor; however each task is assigned to a single processor. Since any intra-task parallelism cannot be exploited upon a single processor, we may ignore the internal structure of the DAG and simply represent such a task τi in the simpler three-parameter sporadic model [23]. A task τj in the threeparameter sporadic model is characterized by the three parameters Cj, Dj and Tj, representing respectively the worstcase execution time, relative deadline, and period parameters of the task. Such a task's jobs are assumed to possess no internal parallelism, but must be executed sequentially upon a single processor. For the purposes of partitioning the light sporadic DAG tasks, each such light conditional sporadic DAG task τi = (Gi, Di, Ti), can therefore be considered as equivalent to a three-parameter sporadic task with worstcase execution time equal to voli, relative deadline Di, and period Ti.

An algorithm for partitioning a specified collection of constrained deadline sporadic three-parameter tasks upon a given multiprocessor platform was derived in [11]. This algorithm, presented in pseudo-code form in Figure 4, makes use of the dbf * approximation to the demand bound function (dbf) [12] of a three-parameter sporadic task, which we restate in terms of the parameters of a light conditional sporadic DAG task:
div.formula: dbf * (τi, t) = 0, if t < Di voli + ui × (t -Di), otherwise(3)
div.p: The following result (re-stated here in terms of the parameters of a sporadic DAG task system) was derived in [11, Corollary 1, page 923]:

Lemma 3. If constrained-deadline conditional sporadic DAG task system τ light can be partitioned by an optimal algorithm on mr identical processors each of a particular computing capacity, then partition(τ light , mr) will successfully partition this system upon a platform comprising mr processors that are each (3 -1/mr) times as fast as the original.

Combining Lemmas 2 and 3 and observing that the speedup bound of Lemma 3 is worse (larger) than that of Lemma 2, we immediately have Theorem 1. If constrained-deadline conditional sporadic DAG task system τ can be scheduled by an optimal federated scheduling algorithm on m identical processors each of a particular computing capacity, then FedSched(τ, m) will successfully schedule this system upon a platform comprising m processors that are each (3 -1/m) times as fast as the original.

Proof Sketch: Consider a constrained-deadline conditional sporadic DAG task system τ in which each task τi ∈ τ has voli ≤ Di. Since there are no heavy tasks in τ , Procedure FedSched(τ, m) will partition the entire task system via the call to Procedure partition (see Line 7 of the pseudocode of Figure 3). For this task system τ , therefore, the performance of Procedure FedSched(τ, m) is dictated entirely by its performance in partitioning a constraineddeadline three-parameter sporadic task system, which is as stated in Lemma 3 above.

div.head: SCHEDULABILITY EXPERIMENTS
div.p: We conducted schedulability experiments to emphasize that the speedup bound of Theorem 1 is a very conservative characterization of the efficacy of the federated scheduling Algorithm FedSched. Our schedulability experiments were conducted using randomly-generated task systems in order to obtain a flavor of its more "typical" performance. Although we should not read too much into the results of these experiments since such results are necessarily deeply influenced by the manner in which we generate our task systems, the results do indicate that (as expected) the algorithm's performance is generally significantly superior to the conservative bound of Theorem 1. In particular, Algorithm FedSched tends to schedule task systems in which there are many heavy tasks with a speedup factor that is far smaller (i.e., better) than (3 -1/m); this is only to be expected since each heavy task's individual contribution to speedup is bounded from above by 2 (as asserted by Lemma 2).

Workload generation. We implemented the random generator for sporadic DAG tasks described in [4] (which is a slight modification of the one proposed in [18]). For each generated DAG task, we randomly replaced some individual vertices by canonical conditional constructs, with the DAG within the conditional construct also being generated using the random generator of [4]. By repeating this process of choosing a vertex to replace several times for each taskthe exact number of times is another randomly-generated parameter -we were able to generate tasks with multiple levels of nesting of conditional constructs.

A task system of any desired utilization is obtained from this task generator by repeatedly adding tasks until the desired utilization is achieved; for the last task that is added, the period parameter is adjusted (increased) so that the total system utilization equals the desired utilization.

Experiments conducted, and observations. We designed and conducted several hundred schedulability experiments by assigning different combinations of values to the various parameters that characterize a random task in the generator of [4], as well as two additional parameters characterizing the likelihood of having a conditional construct, and the expected number of levels of nesting. In each experiment (i.e., for each combination of parameter values considered), we generated ten thousand task systems, with utilizations ranging from 1 to 10. For each generated task system, we computed lower and upper bounds on the number of processors that would be needed to successfully schedule the system under partitioned scheduling, as follows.

• Each heavy task τi must be assigned at least voli/Di processors under federated scheduling. An upper bound on the needed number of processors is obtained by running LS on all the precedence-constrained collections of jobs that could be generated by the task's DAG, and taking the largest makespan..
• A lower bound on the number of processors needed for the partitioning phase is given by max t≥0 τ i ∈τ light dbf(τi, t) t
An upper bound is estimated using a result derived in [11, Theorem 2] -details may be found in [11].

We then determined the actual number of processors that is required by FedSched to schedule the task system. (That is, for each randomly-generated τ we determined the smallest m for which FedSched(τ, m) returns a successful federated schedule.) The observed values revealed that at least with regards to the random task generator that we have used in our experiments, the performance of FedSched trends more closely with (i.e., has a similar slope to) the lower bound rather than the upper bound.

div.head: SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS
div.p: Federated scheduling appears to be a natural generalization of partitioned scheduling for such tasks that exhibit internal parallelism and may need to execute upon multiple processors simultaneously. Prior work has considered the federated scheduling of systems of sporadic DAG tasks that contain no conditional constructs; here, we have obtained analogous results concerning the federated scheduling of systems of more general conditional sporadic DAG tasks. As was the case for regular (non-conditional) sporadic DAG task systems, we are able to derive a polynomial-time algorithm for determining the number of processors for each task that needs to execute exclusively upon multiple processors, and a partitioning strategy for those tasks that execute upon a single processor. Our worst-case bounds (Theorem 1) indicate that at least in terms of the speedup metric, there is no loss in going from the three-parameter sporadic tasks model and the non-conditional sporadic DAG tasks model to the more general conditional sporadic DAG tasks modelthe tightest known speedup factor of (3 -1 m ) for sequential sporadic tasks and non-conditional sporadic DAG tasks is seen to hold for conditional sporadic DAG tasks as well.
